Whether the nationwide study has more observations
Employment changes outside the chain, measured over the same period
The total number of regions in which the chain operates
question.commonError: Generalizing a narrow sample directly to the national economy.
question.feedback: A national aggregate includes other employers. Their gains can exceed the chain's losses even if those losses occur in every region.

question.q: Two queue models fit an office before appointments are introduced. One assumes arrivals cluster; the other assumes service is slow. Appointments spread arrivals without changing service time. Which result best distinguishes them?
options: A large wait reduction favors the arrival-clustering explanation
Unchanged service time proves both explanations equally well
The prior fit establishes that slow service caused the queues
Any remaining wait refutes the arrival-clustering explanation
question.commonError: Choosing models by fit alone when mechanisms differ.
question.feedback: Appointments change arrival clustering while service time stays fixed. A large reduction therefore supports clustering as a mechanism, although other sources of waiting may remain.

question.q: A model predicts policy outcomes accurately in several cities, but its proposed mechanism was never measured. What follows?
options: Accurate predictions establish the proposed mechanism locally, though they leave its transfer to other cities uncertain.
Accurate predictions support usefulness in those cities, but competing mechanisms may fit the same outcomes.
Repeated prediction success establishes literal assumptions, though it leaves the mechanism’s policy importance uncertain.
An unmeasured mechanism invalidates the predictions, even if independent outcome data confirm their accuracy.
question.commonError: Treating shared historical fit as proof of one mechanism.
question.feedback: Predictive success is evidence about predictive performance. It does not discriminate between mechanisms that produce the same observable predictions, nor prove every assumption literal.

question.q: In the value-of-money graph, the economy moves from a to b. Velocity may change. A nominal wage rises in the same proportion as the implied price level, with technology and labor supplies unchanged. What is consistent with monetary neutrality?

Prices and the nominal wage double; the real wage is unchanged.
Prices and the nominal wage rise by one-third; the real wage also rises by one-third.
Prices fall by one-quarter, so an unchanged real wage requires a one-quarter nominal-wage increase.
question.commonError: confusing nominal price-level changes with real-output changes
question.feedback: The graph gives value of money 2 at a and 1.5 at b. Their reciprocal price levels are 1/2 and 2/3, a one-third increase. question.q: A monetary expansion lowers rates and raises investment by $40 billion. A separate loss of confidence reduces investment by $25 billion. With MPC = 0.5, what is the net change in aggregate demand?

Left $30 billion: reverse the effect of a net investment increase
Right $15 billion: include both impulses but omit induced spending
Right $30 billion: multiply the net $15 billion autonomous investment rise
question.commonError: stopping at the investment decrease instead of applying the multiplier

question.q: A monetary contraction reduces investment by $40 billion, with MPC = 0.8. A fiscal program adds $200 billion to aggregate demand in total after induced effects. Compare implementing it immediately with implementing it only after the original contraction has ended.
options: Both timings offset exactly because equal dollar effects guarantee equal stabilization
Immediate AD rises $800 billion because the total fiscal effect must be multiplied again
Immediate AD falls $200 billion because fiscal and monetary shifts cannot offset
Immediate effects offset; the delayed program can create excess demand after the original gap closes
question.commonError: using MPC as the multiplier or reading the AD shift backward
question.feedback: The monetary effect is −40/(1 − 0.8) = −$200 billion, so the immediate fiscal total offsets it. If the program arrives after the original gap closes, the same stimulus can create excess demand. A total effect should not be multiplied again.

question.q: A reduction in money supply raises the interest rate when money demand is fixed. Now suppose money demand also falls. Without the relative sizes of the shifts, what can be predicted about the interest-rate and spending responses?
options: Supply contraction alone raises rates; the combined transmission direction remains uncertain.
Supply contraction dominates; rates rise, investment falls and aggregate demand falls.
Demand contraction dominates; rates fall, investment rises and aggregate demand rises.
The contractions cancel; rates, investment and aggregate demand all remain unchanged.
question.commonError: stopping at the investment decline instead of applying the multiplier
question.feedback: A supply reduction puts upward pressure on the rate, while lower money demand puts downward pressure on it. Without their relative sizes, the net rate movement and the resulting investment and AD directions remain uncertain.

Its direction is uncertain because the two forces affect NCO in opposite directions
It appreciates because the interest-rate effect must dominate the risk effect
It depreciates because political risk affects currency demand but not capital flows
question.commonError: Assuming opposing net-capital-outflow effects must exactly offset, or that one must dominate without their magnitudes.
question.feedback: A higher domestic real interest rate tends to reduce net capital outflow and appreciate the currency. Greater political risk tends to raise net capital outflow and depreciate it. Without the magnitudes, the net currency movement is ambiguous.

question.q: A museum has already paid a nonrefundable $30,000 deposit for an exhibit. It can proceed for another $12,000 and earn $9,000, or use the gallery for a lecture series worth $7,000. Which item is the opportunity cost of proceeding?

The $30,000 nonrefundable deposit
The $42,000 total of past and future spending
Zero because the deposit cannot be recovered
question.commonError: Using an irreversible past expenditure instead of the best current alternative.
question.feedback: The deposit is sunk; the lecture series is the best forgone current use.

question.q: A county can assign an emergency team to wildfire prevention valued at $1.4 million, flood preparation valued at $1.1 million, or routine inspections valued at $0.8 million. Political rules require the flood project. What is its opportunity cost?

$1.1 million because that is the chosen project’s value
$0.8 million because routine inspections cost the least
question.commonError: Confusing the chosen project, the least-valued option, or the sum of alternatives with opportunity cost.
question.feedback: The wildfire program is the most valuable feasible alternative forgone.

question.q: Many small firms sell an identical product. Buyers know the prices but have difficulty judging the product’s benefits. Does this information problem necessarily stop firms from taking the market price, and can we still be sure buyers make efficient choices?

question.q: Use the firm panel to calculate the current operating loss. Should the firm keep producing in the short run? If losses persist, how would exit affect the market price?
options: $100; operate because P > AVC, while persistent losses lead to exit and higher market price.
$150; shut down immediately because P < ATC, even though producing covers avoidable cost.
$100; shut down immediately because P < ATC, even though producing covers avoidable cost.
$150; operate because P > AVC, while persistent losses lead to exit and higher market price.
question.feedback: The market sets P = 15; rising MC gives Q = 50. AVC = 10 < P = 15 < ATC = 18, so the operating loss is 150 and shutdown would sacrifice a contribution to fixed cost. Persistent losses induce exit and raise price as market supply contracts.

question.q: A competitive firm has a minimum average variable cost of $14. Compare two separate cost increases: higher unavoidable fixed rent, or an extra $3 of variable cost on every unit. What is the shutdown-price threshold under each change, and which change shifts short-run supply?
options: $14 with higher rent and $17 with variable cost; only variable cost shifts supply.
$18 with higher rent and $21 with variable cost; only variable cost shifts supply.
$17 under either change; both changes shift supply.
$14 under either change; neither change shifts supply.
question.feedback: The shutdown threshold is minimum AVC. Higher fixed rent changes neither AVC nor MC, leaving the threshold at $14. Adding $3 to variable cost per unit raises AVC and MC by $3, so the threshold becomes $17 and short-run supply shifts upward.

question.q: A competitive industry has 40 identical firms. At a price of $25, each initially supplies 12 units. Higher energy costs reduce each firm’s supply at that price to 9 units. With unchanged market demand and no entry, equilibrium price then rises to $28. At its new MR = MC quantity of 10 units, a firm has ATC $30 and AVC $21. Which assessment is correct?
options: Market supply shifted left; the firm operates with a $20 economic loss
Market supply shifted right; the firm earns $70 economic profit
Market supply shifted left; the firm shuts down because P is below ATC
Market supply stayed fixed; the firm earns $30 economic profit
question.feedback: At the original price, industry supply falls from 480 to 360 units, identifying a leftward shift. At the new optimum, profit is (28 - 30) × 10 = -$20; price still exceeds AVC, so the firm operates. A cost shock can raise market price while reducing profit; the profit result requires the stated cost comparison.

review.Notes: Elite or legendary. Cognitive load or reading the question and answers is too high

question.q: Use π = πe − (u − 5) + s, where π is actual inflation, πe is expected inflation, u is unemployment, and s is the number of percentage points a supply shock adds to inflation. Rates are in percent. Actual inflation is 4% and unemployment is 6%. Without knowing s, a student reports expected inflation as exactly 5%. What assumption does this answer require, and how would a positive value of s change the answer?
options: Expected inflation is exactly 4% whenever actual inflation is 4%
A positive value of s implies a higher expectation estimate at the same inflation and unemployment
5% follows only if s=0; a positive value of s implies a lower expectation estimate
5% is exact for every value of s because actual inflation is given
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Expected inflation is exactly 4% whenever actual inflation is 4%” in this phillips curve expectations task.
question.feedback: Rearranging gives πe = 4 + (6 − 5) − s = 5 − s. Expected inflation is 5% only if s = 0. A positive contribution from the supply shock means lower expected inflation at the same actual inflation and unemployment.

question.q: A report defines success only as maximum total surplus. What choice is normative?
options: Calculating total surplus from observed prices and quantities
Selecting total surplus as the sole ranking criterion
Measuring how total surplus changes after the policy
Estimating the policy’s effect on output.
question.commonError: Treating normative as negative or merely controversial.
question.feedback: A normative claim ranks outcomes or says what ought to be done.

question.q: Two analysts agree that an archive plan preserves more records but delays public access. One recommends it; the other rejects it. What additional finding would show a factual disagreement as well as a value disagreement?
options: They agree on the delay but differ on whether it is acceptable
They use the same probabilities but prefer different distributions of access
They assign different probabilities to permanent record loss under the alternative
They give different ethical priority to immediate public access
question.commonError: Classifying a compound argument as wholly positive or wholly normative.
question.feedback: Probabilities of record loss are empirical assessments. The other differences concern how agreed consequences should be valued.

question.q: A price rises while quantity sold also rises. Which inference is best supported?
options: Demand likely increased, but additional evidence is needed if several forces changed.
Supply must have decreased and nothing else changed.
The higher price caused quantity demanded to rise.
Price signals cannot coordinate markets.
question.commonError: Confusing an equilibrium movement with movement along one curve.
question.feedback: A higher price and quantity are consistent with a demand increase, though simultaneous shifts can complicate diagnosis.

question.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes the move from A to B from the shift of PPF0 to PPF1, using the changes shown in the graph?
options: A to B reallocates existing resources and gives up 40 orders of fries; PPF1 expands capacity and raises maximum burger output by 10.
A to B reallocates existing resources and gives up 20 orders of fries; PPF1 expands capacity and raises maximum burger output by 10.
A to B expands productive capacity by giving up 40 orders of fries; PPF1 only reallocates existing resources toward 10 more burgers.
A to B expands productive capacity by giving up 20 orders of fries; PPF1 only reallocates existing resources toward 10 more burgers.
question.imageAlt: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.
question.feedback: Moving from A to B on PPF0 reallocates existing resources: fries fall from 120 to 80 orders, a sacrifice of 40. Shifting to PPF1 expands productive capacity: the burger-axis intercept rises from 50 to 60. Reallocation changes the output mix within existing capacity; an outward shift expands what can be produced.
question.graphDescription: Burgers are on the horizontal axis and fries on the vertical axis. Bowed PPF0 includes A at 10 burgers and 120 fries and B at 30 burgers and 80 fries. Dashed PPF1 lies outside PPF0, reaching about 150 fries at zero burgers and 60 burgers at zero fries.

question.q: Starting at the original equilibrium, the Fed increases money supply. Which complete chain is correct?
options: MS shifts right, excess money appears at the old price level, spending rises, P rises, and the value of money falls.
MS shifts left, excess money appears, spending rises, P falls, and the value of money rises.
MD shifts right, money supply stays fixed, P falls, and value of money rises.
MS shifts right, spending falls, P falls, and the value of money rises.
question.commonError: getting the direction of value of money backward
question.feedback: A monetary injection shifts MS right. At the old price level there is excess money, which fuels spending, raises P, and lowers the value of money.

question.q: If the economy moves from the original equilibrium to the new equilibrium after a monetary injection, why does the price level rise rather than output permanently rise in the long-run model?
options: Real factors determine long-run output; extra money mainly raises prices.
Money demand becomes vertical and real output doubles.
The Fed directly raises real GDP by shifting MD right.
The price level rises because the value of money rises.
question.commonError: thinking monetary injection permanently raises real output in the long-run money market model
question.feedback: In the long-run model, real output is determined by real factors, so more money mainly raises the price level.

question.q: At the old equilibrium value of money after MS shifts right, what disequilibrium exists and what removes it?
options: Excess supply of money; people spend or lend excess balances until prices rise.
Excess demand for money; people sell goods until prices fall.
Excess supply of goods; people hoard money until the price level falls.
No disequilibrium; the value of money changes without behavior.
question.commonError: missing why prices rise after excess money appears
question.feedback: At the old price level, the higher money supply creates excess money balances. People spend or lend them, pushing prices up.

review.Notes: hard or elite

question.q: A country has nominal spending $960. It aims for a 3% price-level increase with real output up 2% and velocity down 1%. What money-growth rate is required, and why is adding 3% and 2% incomplete?
options: About 4.0% money growth; falling velocity amplifies the desired spending increase
Exactly 1% money growth; subtract real growth from the price target
About 6.1% money growth; falling velocity also has to be offset
Exactly 5% money growth; velocity does not affect the target
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “About 4.0% money growth; falling velocity amplifies the desired spending increase” in this quantity theory of money task.
question.feedback: Solve M factor = P factor × Y factor / V factor = 1.03×1.02/.99≈1.06121, or 6.1%. The velocity decline reduces spending per dollar and requires additional money growth.

review.Topic: Real Exchange Rates and Purchasing Power

question.q: Domestic inflation exceeds foreign inflation for several years, yet the real exchange rate is nearly unchanged. What nominal pattern is consistent with this outcome?
options: A nominal depreciation too small to offset the inflation differential
A nominal depreciation that offsets the inflation differential
A nominal appreciation equal to the inflation differential
A fixed nominal exchange rate regardless of the inflation gap
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “A nominal depreciation too small to offset the inflation differential” in this real exchange rates and purchasing power task.
question.feedback: To stabilize eP/P*, faster domestic price growth must be offset by a lower e, a nominal depreciation.

question.commonError: Forgetting that the GDP deflator compares nominal GDP to real GDP.
question.q: Real GDP rises 5% while nominal GDP rises 15.5%. What happens to the GDP deflator, and by how much does real production rise?
options: Deflator rises 10%; real production rose 5%
Deflator rises 10.5%; real production rose 15.5%
Deflator rises 20.5%; real production rose 5%
Deflator is unchanged; the two growth rates use different units
question.feedback: The price-index ratio is 1.155/1.05 = 1.10. Thus the deflator rises 10%, while the stated real production increase remains 5%. Price and quantity growth combine multiplicatively.

question.q: Households reduce current consumption and buy a firm's newly issued bonds. The firm uses the proceeds for new machinery and to purchase an existing office building. Which chain is economically correct?
options: Both firm purchases are current GDP investment because both use borrowed funds
The bond purchase is physical investment, while neither firm purchase enters GDP
Household saving enters GDP directly, and the machinery is only a financial asset
Saving finances the firm, but only the new machinery is current GDP investment
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both firm purchases are current GDP investment because both use borrowed funds” in this saving and investment identities task.
question.feedback: The bond market channels household saving to the borrower. New machinery is current production and GDP investment; transferring an existing building is not new production.

question.q: At every given real interest rate, planned private saving increases by $25 billion, but a larger deficit reduces public saving by $40 billion. With investment demand unchanged, which sequence follows?
options: National saving rises by $65 billion; supply shifts right, the real rate falls, and investment rises
National saving falls by $15 billion; supply shifts left, the real rate rises, and investment falls
National saving falls by $15 billion; investment demand shifts left, lowering both rate and quantity
National saving rises by $15 billion; supply shifts right, but investment necessarily falls
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “National saving rises by $65 billion; supply shifts right, the real rate falls, and investment rises” in this saving and investment identities task.
question.feedback: The public-saving decline is larger than the private-saving increase, so national saving falls by $15 billion. Supply shifts left, raising financing costs and crowding out investment along demand.

question.q: In a closed economy, at every given real interest rate, planned private saving rises by $20 billion while public saving falls by $35 billion. At the same time, new technology raises desired investment. What can be concluded without knowing how much investment demand increases?
options: Both curves shift right; quantity rises, while the real rate is ambiguous
Supply shifts left only; both the real rate and quantity must fall
Investment demand shifts right only; the real rate rises and quantity must rise
Supply shifts left, demand shifts right; the rate rises and quantity is ambiguous
question.commonError: Incorrectly concludes “Both curves shift right; quantity rises, while the real rate is ambiguous” in this saving and investment identities task.
question.feedback: At each given real rate, planned national saving falls by $15 billion, shifting supply left. Technology shifts investment demand right. Both shifts raise the real rate, but their quantity effects oppose one another; the final change in realized saving and investment is therefore not fixed at −$15 billion.

question.q: A policy improves equity but reduces total surplus. Which answer best frames the issue?
options: It presents an efficiency-equity tradeoff requiring both criteria
It proves the policy is desirable because equity necessarily dominates
It proves the policy is undesirable because total surplus necessarily dominates
It removes scarcity because one distributional goal improves
question.feedback: Policies often involve tradeoffs. A reduction in efficiency may or may not be justified by equity goals.

question.q: A coastal city can use a limited parcel for flood protection, affordable housing, or commercial development. Which analysis best respects scarcity?
options: Compare feasible parcel uses, incremental benefits and displaced uses, making the distribution of gains and losses explicit.
Rank uses by expected cash revenue, counting public benefits only when the city can charge users for them.
Rank uses by the number of beneficiaries, treating benefit size and displaced alternatives as secondary tie-breakers.
Divide the parcel equally among uses, treating equal area shares as sufficient evidence of equal benefit and efficiency.
question.commonError: Listing benefits without confronting mutually exclusive uses.
question.feedback: A scarce parcel requires a feasible comparison of valued uses, including nonmarket benefits and distribution. Cash revenue, beneficiary counts or equal acreage alone can miss opportunity costs and competing criteria.

question.q: Workers expect 6 percent inflation, but actual inflation is 2 percent and wage contracts reflect the higher expectation. What happens to SRAS relative to contracts based on accurate expectations?
options: Contract nominal wages are lower and real labor costs at actual prices are lower; SRAS lies farther right
Contract nominal wages are lower and real labor costs at actual prices are higher; SRAS lies farther left
Contract nominal wages are higher and real labor costs at actual prices are higher; SRAS lies farther left
Contract nominal wages are higher and real labor costs at actual prices are lower; SRAS lies farther right
question.commonError: Ignoring how excessive expected inflation enters wage contracts.
question.feedback: Higher expected prices can produce higher nominal wages and lower short-run supply.

question.q: A severe storm destroys capital, while emergency deregulation lowers current compliance costs. Which conclusion is strongest?
options: Capital destruction reduces LRAS; cost relief shifts only AD, so the SRAS direction is certainly left
Capital destruction reduces LRAS; its adverse SRAS effect competes with lower compliance costs, leaving net SRAS uncertain
Capital destruction reduces LRAS; lower compliance costs also reduce SRAS, so both short-run forces shift supply left
Lower compliance costs raise LRAS; capital destruction affects only SRAS, so long-run capacity rises
question.commonError: Assuming all supply forces have the same horizon and direction.
question.feedback: Capital destruction lowers capacity; lower compliance cost pushes SRAS right, while storm disruption may push it left.

question.q: Two economies experience the same rise in actual output prices. In A, wages and expected prices remain fixed; in B, wage contracts reset upward with expectations. A student predicts identical output responses because actual prices changed equally. What is missing?
options: A moves along its existing SRAS, while B's higher expected costs also shift SRAS left, restraining its output response.
Both actual-price increases shift SRAS right by the same amount, so wage-setting differences cannot matter.
Only B moves along SRAS; fixed wages in A force an immediate rightward LRAS shift.
B's higher expected wage costs shift SRAS right, reinforcing the output effect of the actual-price rise.
question.commonError: Confusing movement along SRAS with a curve shift.
question.feedback: Actual prices are the vertical-axis variable: changing them moves along a given supply schedule. Changed expectations and wage costs alter that schedule. Equal observed price changes therefore need not imply equal output responses under different contract conditions.

question.q: Refer to the concert graph with Demand with tax. The law changes so sellers remit the same tax instead. With demand and supply fixed, which cash-flow description fits the resulting equilibrium?
options: Buyers pay sellers $8; sellers remit $8 and keep $0; 150,000 tickets trade
Buyers pay sellers $18; sellers remit $8 and keep $10; 200,000 tickets trade
Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $8 and keep $8; 150,000 tickets trade
Buyers pay sellers $16; sellers remit $6 and keep $10; 200,000 tickets trade
question.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.
question.feedback: The graph shows buyer cost $16 and net seller receipt $8 at 150,000 tickets, so the wedge is $8. Switching remittance changes the transaction payment, not these net prices or quantity. Sellers now collect $16, forward $8 and retain $8.
question.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Demand with tax intersects supply at quantity 150 and seller price 8; original demand there gives buyer price 16.

question.q: The movie tax in the graph is currently collected from buyers. Collection shifts to sellers, with the tax, demand, supply, and compliance unchanged. A cinema proposes adding the tax again to the buyer’s current total payment. Which corrected tax-inclusive invoice and burden calculation preserve the competitive outcome?
options: Invoice $13.50; buyers bear $2 and sellers $4
Invoice $12.50; buyers bear $2 and sellers $4
Invoice $12.50; buyers bear $3 and sellers $3
Invoice $13.50; buyers bear $3 and sellers $3
question.feedback: The graph shows a $6 tax, a $7.50 net seller receipt, and a $13.50 total buyer price, compared with $10.50 before tax. After the collection change the invoice remains $13.50 including tax; the seller remits $6 and keeps $7.50. Each side bears $3. Adding another $6 would charge the tax twice.

question.q: A product gets more expensive because demand increases. Sellers produce more at the higher price. Students say supply increased. What is the error?
options: They confused an increase in quantity supplied with an increase in supply
They correctly identified a supply shift
They confused demand with quantity demanded
They ignored that equilibrium cannot change
question.feedback: Sellers move along the supply curve when price rises. Quantity supplied increases, but supply does not shift.

question.q: A new machine lowers unit production cost, while a new per-unit environmental fee raises cost. Which conclusion about supply is justified without knowing the size of each change?
options: Supply must shift right because improved technology outweighs any higher per-unit fee.
Supply must shift left because a new per-unit fee outweighs any technological saving.
Supply must remain unchanged because there is one cost decrease and one cost increase.
The net supply shift cannot be determined without comparing the two cost changes.
question.commonError: Assuming one opposing supply shifter automatically dominates the other.
question.feedback: The cost saving increases supply; the fee reduces supply. The net direction depends on the magnitudes, not the number of changes.

question.q: Twenty new firms enter a market, but an essential input becomes more expensive for every firm. What is the most careful conclusion about market supply?
options: Entry pushes supply right and higher input cost pushes it left, leaving the net effect uncertain.
Market supply must rise because entry outweighs the input-cost increase.
Market supply must fall because higher input costs outweigh entry.
Market supply stays fixed because both events only change quantity supplied along the curve.
question.commonError: Ignoring an offsetting change in the number of sellers or input costs.
question.feedback: More firms add supply at each price; a cost increase reduces each firm’s supply. Without magnitudes, the combined shift can go either way or be zero.

question.q: Compare the initial point on S0 at $9 with the final point on S1 at $13. Which explanation separates the supply change from the later price change?
options: The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand without shifting supply back.
The supply decrease reduces quantity from 250 to 150 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 250 thousand without shifting supply back.
The supply decrease reduces quantity from 200 to 100 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 200 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
The supply decrease reduces quantity from 250 to 150 thousand at $9; the price rise moves along S1 to 250 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
question.feedback: At $9, S0 shows 200 thousand units and S1 shows 100 thousand. The lower quantity at the same price is a supply decrease. A subsequent price rise to $13 moves along S1 to 200 thousand. Returning to the original quantity does not shift supply back to S0.

question.q: Compare A on S0 with the final point on S1 at $2. Which explanation separates the supply change from the later price change?
options: The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand without shifting supply back.
The supply increase raises quantity from 125 to about 250 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 125 thousand without shifting supply back.
The supply increase raises quantity from 100 to about 225 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 100 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
The supply increase raises quantity from 125 to about 250 thousand at A’s price; the price fall moves along S1 to about 125 thousand because supply shifts back to S0.
question.feedback: A is at $3 and 100 thousand tacos on S0. At that same price, S1 shows about 225 thousand, indicating a supply increase. The later price fall to $2 moves along S1 to about 100 thousand. Quantity returns to its original level, but the supply curve remains S1.

question.q: Using the original equilibrium and the after-tax buyer and seller prices, which burden split and relative-elasticity conclusion fit the graph?
options: Buyers bear $5 and sellers $3; demand is less elastic
Buyers bear $2 and sellers $6; supply is less elastic
Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2; demand is less elastic
Buyers bear $3 and sellers $5; supply is less elastic
question.imageAlt: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.
question.feedback: The original price is $10, the buyer price is $16, and the net seller price is $8. Buyers bear $6 and sellers $2 of the $8 tax. The larger buyer burden indicates less elastic demand over this change.
question.graphDescription: The concert-ticket market has price vertically and quantity in thousands horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 16; original supply there gives seller price 8.

question.q: Refer to the graph. Which side bears more of the $8 tax, and what does that imply about relative elasticity?
options: Buyers bear 6 dollars; demand is less elastic
Sellers bear 2 dollars; supply is more elastic
Buyers bear all 8 dollars; demand is perfectly inelastic
Sellers bear $6; supply is less elastic.
question.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.
question.feedback: The seller price falls by $6 while the buyer price rises by $2. Sellers therefore bear more of the tax, consistent with supply being less elastic than demand.
question.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.

question.q: The $8 tax is legally collected from sellers. Using the original equilibrium as the benchmark, which division of the economic burden does the graph show?
options: Buyers bear $2 per unit; sellers bear $6 per unit
Buyers bear $3 per unit; sellers bear $5 per unit
Buyers bear $6 per unit; sellers bear $2 per unit
Buyers bear $5 per unit; sellers bear $3 per unit
question.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.
question.feedback: The original price is $10. After the tax, buyers pay $12 and sellers keep $4. Buyers therefore bear $2 and sellers $6. Legal collection from sellers does not determine the economic division.
question.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and steep S0 intersect at A, quantity 200 and price 10 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 150 and buyer price 12; original supply there gives seller price 4.

question.q: A tax is imposed on a good with highly inelastic demand and elastic supply. Which policy outcome is most likely?
options: Buyers bear most of the burden and quantity falls relatively little
Sellers bear most of the burden and quantity falls dramatically
Buyers bear no burden because sellers legally pay
The tax creates a surplus equal to the tax
question.feedback: Inelastic demand means buyers bear more and reduce quantity less in response to the tax.

question.q: Before a tax, price is $40 and 500 units trade. Afterward buyers pay $46, sellers keep $34, and 420 units trade. What is the buyers’ tax burden on the units still traded, as distinct from the entire change in consumer surplus?
question.feedback: The per-unit buyer burden is $46 − $40 = $6. On 420 continuing units, its rectangle is $2,520. The full CS change also includes lost gains from the 80 missing trades; the rectangle alone does not measure that entire loss.

question.q: A market moves from $40 and 500 units before a tax to a buyer price of $46, seller receipt of $34, and 420 units afterward. On the units still sold after the tax, what is the sellers’ total loss from receiving a lower price? Exclude surplus lost on sales that no longer occur.
question.feedback: The seller loses $40 − $34 = $6 per continuing unit, so the rectangle is $6 × 420 = $2,520. Using 500 applies the burden to trades that no longer occur. The $12 wedge times 420 is total revenue, not the seller share alone.

question.q: A tax is imposed on sellers. Before the tax, price is $20 and quantity is 300. After the tax, buyers pay $24, sellers receive $18, and quantity is 240. Which statement is correct?
options: Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $2 per unit; seller burden: $4 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $0 per unit; seller burden: $6 per unit; quantity falls by 60 units.
Tax wedge: $6; buyer burden: $4 per unit; seller burden: $2 per unit; quantity falls by 240 units.
question.feedback: The tax wedge is $24 - $18 = $6 per unit. Relative to the original $20 price, buyers bear $24 - $20 = $4 per unit and sellers bear $20 - $18 = $2 per unit; these burdens sum to $6. Quantity falls by 300 - 240 = 60 units. The 240 units are the new quantity, not the decrease. Requiring sellers to remit the tax does not make them bear its entire economic burden.

question.q: Suppose the per-trip tax shown is halved while demand and supply stay fixed. Calculate tax revenue before and after the change. Does the increase in trips fully offset the lower tax per trip?
options: $600,000 to $350,000; extra trips offset part, but not all, of the lower tax rate.
$800,000 to $450,000; extra trips offset part, but not all, of the lower tax rate.
$800,000 to $450,000; a tax-rate cut leaves the number of trips fixed by definition.
$600,000 to $350,000; a tax-rate cut leaves the number of trips fixed by definition.
question.imageAlt: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.
question.feedback: The original tax wedge is 14−10 = 4 at 200 thousand trips; untaxed Q is 250 thousand. Halving the tax to 2 moves quantity halfway to 250, or 225 thousand, under the fixed linear curves. Receipts change 4 × 200,000 = 800,000 to 2 × 225,000 = 450,000. The quantity response partially offsets the rate cut.
question.graphDescription: The rideshare market has price per trip vertically and quantity in thousands per day horizontally. D0 and S0 intersect at A, quantity 250 and price 12 dollars. Supply with tax intersects demand at quantity 200 and buyer price 14; original supply there gives seller price 10.

question.q: A luxury tax causes quantity sold to fall sharply and tax revenue disappoints. What is the strongest explanation?
options: A strong response to the tax-related price change sharply reduces trade
The tax must be too small to affect purchases and sales
Buyers must bear the entire burden, leaving sellers unaffected by the tax
Imposing a tax always increases total revenue regardless of market responses
question.feedback: If market participants respond strongly, quantity falls sharply and tax revenue may be lower than expected.

question.q: Refer to the movie-tax graph. A report counts only the buyer price increase as the tax rate. Which correction correctly gives the two per-unit burdens and total government revenue?
options: Buyers bear $2 and sellers $2; revenue is $400,000
Buyers bear $2 and sellers $2; revenue is $560,000
Buyers bear $4 and sellers $0; revenue is $400,000
Buyers bear $2 and sellers $0; revenue is $200,000
question.feedback: The old price is $12, buyer price $14 and seller receipt $10. Thus the burdens are $2 each, summing to the $4 wedge. Apply that wedge to 100,000 taxed units: revenue is $400,000. The old quantity of 140,000 no longer trades.

question.commonError: Classifying people by desire for work instead of paid work and active search status.
question.q: A survey has 84 adults working for pay, including 14 seeking more hours; 6 available jobless adults applied last week; 30 jobless adults are not searching. Which official count and limitation are correct?
options: Labor force 90 and unemployment about 6.7%; underemployment among paid workers is not in that rate
Labor force 104 and unemployment about 19.2%; add those seeking more hours to unemployment
Labor force 120 and unemployment 5%; use every adult in the denominator
Labor force 76 and unemployment about 7.9%; exclude part-time paid workers
question.feedback: All 84 paid workers are employed, including those wanting more hours. Add the 6 active, available seekers for LF = 90; 6/90 ≈ 6.7%. The rate does not measure all of the part-time workers’ unmet demand for hours.
